answer:
**Cold start means missing evidence, not evidence of dislike.** A new user has no interaction history, while a new item has no learned engagement record. The system needs useful initial representations and a controlled way to gather feedback. [1](https://research.google/pubs/sampling-bias-corrected-neural-modeling-for-large-corpus-item-recommendations/) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)

For users, use current session actions, stated interests, context, and a diverse quality prior. A first search for hiking boots is more informative than treating the user as an average of all established users. For items, content embeddings from text, images, or audio can place a new upload near related items before its ID embedding is well trained.

**Exploration creates the missing evidence.** A contextual bandit balances estimated utility with uncertainty. UCB adds an uncertainty bonus; Thompson sampling samples plausible reward parameters and acts under that sampled model. Both require a meaningful uncertainty model and careful feedback logging. Exploration should remain within quality and eligibility constraints.

Meta-learning may help when many related adaptation tasks and few-shot assumptions match deployment, but it is not required for a strong baseline. Track cold-start cohorts separately, including useful first exposure and subsequent satisfaction. A global score dominated by established traffic can conceal total failure on new users or creators. Do not equate unexposed items with observed negative feedback.

**Technical details and references.**

For new users, use session/context features, stated preferences, locale, and safe popularity/diversity priors, then update from early interactions. For new items, encode text/image/audio and metadata so retrieval does not depend solely on an untrained ID embedding. [1](https://research.google/pubs/sampling-bias-corrected-neural-modeling-for-large-corpus-item-recommendations/) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)

Contextual bandits allocate bounded exploration according to uncertainty and expected utility; record actual propensities for evaluation. Meta-learning can accelerate adaptation when tasks and few-shot assumptions fit, but is not a prerequisite or guaranteed improvement.

Separate lack of evidence from negative preference. Protect users from low-quality or unsafe exploratory items and enforce creator/tenant eligibility. Evaluate cold-start cohorts explicitly, including time-to-first-useful-exposure and long-term quality; a global metric dominated by established users/items can hide failure.
